clue.text: Strong draught horse, obviously

parts.note: a breed of heavy farm horse from an East Anglian county, whose second name is also a strong mixed drink, so a 'strong draught' in two senses

explanation.surface: A remark that a powerful cart-horse is plainly what it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draught' reads as pulling carts, but also as a drink, and a punch is a strong drink. Suffolk is a county in eastern England that gives its name to this breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The breed is a heavy chestnut farm horse bred for hauling ploughs and carts.

clue.text: Take wine to keep up one's strength

parts.note: to sup is to take food or drink by mouthfuls
port is a fortified wine from Portugal

explanation.surface: Advice to have a glass of wine to keep your energy up.
explanation.definitionFit: To bolster or hold up something, keeping it from weakening, is to bear it up.

clue.text: Singular person 'employed in writing autobiography

parts.note: grammar names 'I' the singular person of this rank, the one used when a writer tells their own life story

explanation.surface: A remark about an odd individual hired to ghost-write a memoir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular person' reads as an eccentric, but it is the grammatical person 'I', which an autobiography is written in.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar ranks 'I' as the opening person, the one an autobiographer writes in.

clue.text: Former pupils making good in hiding

parts.note: old boys, abbreviated OBS, are former pupils of a school
curing is making well or remedying

explanation.surface: Old school alumni put right a place of concealment.
explanation.definitionFit: Concealing something from view is keeping it in darkness or cover.

clue.text: Break for a little sound sleep ?

indicators.note: the word sound tells us the word for sleep is to be heard, giving a word spelt differently

parts.note: a nap is a short sleep

explanation.surface: Taking a pause in order to get a short restful doze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a little' qualifies the sleep as a short one; 'sound' looks like part of 'sound sleep' but signals the homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: To knap is to strike and split flint or stones, an old verb for breaking.

clue.text: This for a girl not otherwise engaged

definitions.text: This for a girl not otherwise engaged

parts.words: This for a girl not otherwise engaged
parts.note: a girl with no fiance is not yet claimed: the phrase for that, with 'for' after it, describes her

explanation.surface: A description of a young woman who has no other commitments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engaged' reads as busy, but it means betrothed; a girl not betrothed is 'unspoken for'.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman not promised in marriage is said to be 'unspoken for', not yet claimed.

clue.text: It struck one a squeaker was on the run here

definitions.text: It struck one a squeaker was on the run here

parts.words: It struck one a squeaker was on the run here
parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Hickory Dickory Dock, a mouse runs up a timepiece, which then strikes one

explanation.surface: Someone realising that an informer had escaped from this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeaker' reads as an informer and 'struck one' as an idea occurring, but it is the mouse of the nursery rhyme, and the hour struck.
explanation.definitionFit: The timepiece in the rhyme strikes one and the mouse runs down.

clue.text: Bond with glue somehow to make it stick

indicators.note: somehow tells us the letters of the two words are put together in some new way

explanation.surface: Fixing something with adhesive in some way so it stays put.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges BOND and GLUE. 'Stick' looks like the verb for gluing, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy club with a thickened end is a cudgel or weapon stick.

clue.text: Good man, always right, he's no drop-out

parts.note: ST, saint, is the crossword good man
aye is an old word for always or ever

explanation.surface: Praise for a reliable, consistently correct fellow who never quits.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse or person with endurance lasts the course rather than falling away.

clue.text: One's surrounded by Greek islanders, capital fellows

indicators.note: surrounded by tells us the first piece is placed within the second

parts.note: Parians are natives of Paros, an island in the Cyclades
one is I and the 's is IS, one is

explanation.surface: A person among inhabitants of a Greek isle, all fine people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital fellows' reads as splendid chaps, but means natives of a capital city, France's.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhabitants of France's capital city are men of that capital.

clue.text: Wise little thing to throw in the towel

indicators.note: to throw letters in is to toss them about, so the word that follows is scrambled

explanation.surface: A young sage on the point of giving up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'throw in the towel' reads as surrender, but it scrambles TOWEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A young bird of the species famed for wisdom is a small wise creature.

clue.text: Production for, export only ?

parts.note: goods produced are what is put out, and goods for export are sent out of the country

explanation.surface: A factory slogan: we make goods solely to send abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer split in two: what is put out is the 'production', which ties to sending goods out.
explanation.definitionFit: The amount a factory or worker produces is their yield.

clue.text: Routine, but not for the night shift

definitions.text: Routine, but not for the night shift

parts.words: Routine, but not for the night shift
parts.note: an adjective for ordinary, which split up says labour during daylight hours, not overnight

explanation.surface: A dull schedule that excludes working overnight.
explanation.walkthrough: Split, the answer reads 'work a day', which a night-shift worker does not.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyday and ordinary things are humdrum and routine.

clue.text: Morsel a bird pecked

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
bit, past tense of bite, means pecked

explanation.surface: A small bird pecking at a scrap of food.
explanation.definitionFit: A tasty small piece of food is a tidbit or snippet.

clue.text: Assiduous, albeit lacking polish

parts.note: tho is a shortened form of though, meaning albeit
rough means unrefined, lacking polish

explanation.surface: Hardworking, though somewhat unrefined.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone painstaking and careful leaves nothing undone.

clue.text: Pick fruit, come again

parts.note: to reap is to gather or pick a crop
a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: An invitation to come back and pick fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: To show up once more after being gone is to return into view.

clue.text: Powerfully rich underworld. leader many desert

parts.note: Pluto is the Roman god who rules the underworld
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many
to rat is to desert or betray

explanation.surface: A mighty gangland boss whom many followers abandon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'underworld leader' reads as a crime boss, but means the ruler of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A person whose power comes from great wealth is a moneyed ruler.

clue.text: Boxed all-round bounder, but fell, wetly

indicators.note: all-round says the first word wraps right round the second

parts.note: cased means boxed, put in a case
a cad is a bounder, a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A boxer surrounded by a rotter, yet knocked down in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxed' and 'bounder' suggest sport and leaping, but give CASED and CAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that tumbled down in stages like a waterfall dropped in a wet way.

clue.text: Circle Hamburg wildly in a carriage

indicators.note: wildly tells us these letters run riot into a fresh order

parts.note: a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Driving around a German city in a horse-drawn coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A closed four-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle, named after Lord Brougham.

clue.text: Tavern that serves up food scraps — same place

indicators.note: in a down clue, serves up says the pieces are written from bottom to top

parts.note: orts are scraps of leftover food
ib, short for ibidem, means in the same place

explanation.surface: An inn that offers diners leftovers, in the same spot as before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'serves up' turns the whole run ORTSIB upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A small inexpensive restaurant or wine bar is a modern tavern.

clue.text: Underground timekeeper ?

parts.note: a root vegetable grows below ground, and the same name was slang for a bulky old pocket watch

explanation.surface: A clock-watcher working on the London Tube.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underground' suggests the Tube but means growing in the soil; the vegetable's name was old slang for a big pocket watch.
explanation.definitionFit: The root grows in the earth, and old slang used its name for a fat watch.

clue.text: Olivine found by one small spot

parts.note: per means by, as in per post
I is the Roman numeral one
a dot is a small spot

explanation.surface: A green gemstone discovered by a person with a tiny mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The gem is the green gem-quality variety of the mineral olivine.

clue.text: Tap with a crowbar ?

parts.note: a valve in a pipe, read whimsically as a rooster that halts crowing, a bar to the crow

explanation.surface: Striking something lightly with a metal lever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crowbar' is split as 'crow bar': a cock that stops crowing; the tap is a valve.
explanation.definitionFit: A valve fitted in a water pipe to shut off the flow.

clue.text: Badly cared for framework

indicators.note: badly says the letters of the next word are poorly arranged

explanation.surface: A badly looked-after structure.
explanation.definitionFit: A core group or structure around which an organisation is built.

clue.text: Oh — the flowers that bloom in the spring" (Gilbert)

definitions.text: Oh — the flowers that bloom in the spring" (Gilbert)

parts.words: Oh — the flowers that bloom in the spring" (Gilbert)
parts.note: a line from W S Gilbert's lyric in The Mikado, with the dash standing for the missing word of annoyance

explanation.surface: A quoted line from a Gilbert and Sullivan song about spring flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the blank from the Mikado song 'The Flowers that Bloom in the Spring'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a mild exclamation of annoyance, a cussword like 'drat'.

clue.text: Why the loss of capital from old port ?

indicators.note: capital means the first letter, so the loss of capital drops the opening letter

parts.note: the letters run on in these words only because the clue removes the leading W, a deletion rather than a hidden word, so this is a coincidence of the device

explanation.surface: Asking why an old harbour town lost its money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' suggests money, but means the initial letter W of 'Why'. Hythe in Kent is one of the Cinque Ports, a medieval league of English Channel harbours.
explanation.definitionFit: Hythe in Kent was one of the medieval Cinque Ports.

clue.text: A shade from. The Cruel Sea

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A colour taken from a famous war novel's title.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cruel Sea is a Second World War novel by Nicholas Monsarrat.
explanation.definitionFit: The pale greyish-yellow colour of unbleached linen is a shade.

clue.text: Dress I'd regard as stiff

parts.note: to rig out is to dress
I'd without its apostrophe gives the letters

explanation.surface: Someone regards an outfit as starchy.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbending and inflexible things are rigid or stiff.

clue.text: Last month made a speech and was honoured

parts.note: DEC, December, is the last month
orated means made a speech

explanation.surface: Someone gave an address last month and received an award.
explanation.definitionFit: Receiving a medal or award means receiving an honour.

clue.text: Fresh arrangement by Wallace's four in trade mix-up

indicators.note: in says one piece is put inside the other
a mix-up of letters means they are scrambled

parts.note: Edgar Wallace wrote the thriller The Four Just Men

explanation.surface: A new layout of four of Wallace's characters amid a commercial muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Four Just Men is a 1905 thriller by Edgar Wallace, so 'Wallace's four' are the just men; 'mix-up' scrambles the trade letters to READT before 'in' places them round.
explanation.definitionFit: A rearrangement or adjustment made anew is a fresh arrangement.
